claims.text: The initial Mg-containing lightweight HEA is in a non-equilibrium, metastable solid-solution-containing state.
Isothermal annealing at approximately 500°C for 0.5, 2, and 6 hours is the proposed intervention.
Using an inert atmosphere will eliminate concurrent surface oxidation effects during annealing.
The selected annealing durations simulate different service exposures.
Mg atoms locally enrich or segregate within the metastable solid solution.
Localized Mg enrichment produces discrete Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates within the matrix.
The intermetallic precipitates form through diffusion-controlled nucleation and growth.
Increasing annealing time increases the number density and volume fraction of Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates.
There is a critical intermetallic volume fraction above which functional properties begin to degrade.
Once the critical intermetallic content is reached, uniform passive-film formation and film protectiveness are compromised.
Higher intermetallic volume fractions reduce corrosion resistance relative to the initial metastable state.
Intermetallic precipitation alters high-temperature oxidation pathways.
Samples with higher intermetallic volume fractions will have lower high-temperature oxidation resistance than the initial metastable state.
The proposed transformation and degradation mechanism is expected to apply near 500°C when exposure is long enough to trigger diffusion-driven intermetallic formation.
The mechanism may not apply outside the stated temperature and duration regime.
The degradation threshold may depend on compositional variation and local microstructural heterogeneity.
An unannealed sample set provides the controlled baseline for comparison with annealed samples.

The hypothesis is falsified if extended annealing does not significantly increase discrete Mg-rich intermetallic precipitation or if corrosion and oxidation performance remains statistically indistinguishable from the initial state.

contradictions.description: The conditions broadly state that experiments are conducted in an inert atmosphere to eliminate oxidation, while the outcome and measurements require high-temperature oxidation tests. This is operationally inconsistent unless the inert-atmosphere condition is explicitly limited to the annealing stage.

Property degradation is said to require an unknown critical intermetallic fraction and a sufficiently long exposure, but statistically unchanged properties after the fixed annealing schedule are declared falsifying without first establishing that the critical fraction or sufficient-duration condition was reached.
